title: The Isoperimetric Theorem
description: Among all curves of a given perimeter, the circle encloses the maximum area. Equivalently, among all shapes of a given area, the circle has minimum perimeter.

meta.author: Ancient Greeks, rigorous proof by Weierstrass (1870s)
originalContributions: Framework for perimeter and area of planar curves
meta.assumptions: 1 axiom: isoperimetric_inequality. See Lean source for complete statement.

overview.historicalContext: The isoperimetric problem is one of the oldest in mathematics. According to Virgil's *Aeneid* (29–19 BCE), Queen Dido of Carthage was promised as much land as a bull's hide could encompass; she cut it into thin strips and formed a semicircle against the coast, maximizing the enclosed area. The ancient Greeks knew the circle was optimal, and Zenodorus (~200 BCE) gave geometric arguments. The first attempt at a rigorous proof was by Jakob Steiner (1838) using his **symmetrization** method, but this assumed the optimal curve exists. Karl Weierstrass (1870s) filled this gap using the direct method of the calculus of variations. Adolf Hurwitz (1902) gave an elegant proof via **Fourier analysis** and the Wirtinger inequality. The Brunn-Minkowski inequality (1887–1896) provides yet another route. The theorem generalizes to Riemannian manifolds, where Lévy and Gromov established isoperimetric comparisons, and to metric measure spaces via Lott-Sturm-Villani theory.
overview.problemStatement:
**Isoperimetric Theorem**: For any simple closed curve with perimeter L enclosing area A:

$$4\pi A \leq L^2$$

Equality holds if and only if the curve is a circle.
overview.text: A 449-line axiomatized formalization of the isoperimetric inequality $4\pi A \leq L^2$ with 32 declarations, 0 sorries. Defines `ClosedCurve` (parameterized by arc length), `enclosed_area` (via Green's theorem), and `perimeter`. The main inequality is axiomatized (full proof requires Wirtinger's inequality or Brunn-Minkowski). Proves `circle_achieves_equality` ($4\pi \cdot \pi r^2 = (2\pi r)^2$), `isoperimetric_quotient` ($Q = 4\pi A/L^2 \leq 1$ with equality iff circle), and applications to regular $n$-gons (`regular_polygon_quotient` approaching 1 as $n \to \infty$). Includes Steiner symmetrization lemma and Queen Dido's problem as commentary. Axioms encode the curve-theoretic inequality and the equality characterization.
overview.proofStrategy: Modern proofs use calculus of variations, Fourier analysis, or the Brunn-Minkowski inequality. The key is showing that any deviation from circular shape decreases the area-to-perimeter ratio.
keyInsights: The circle is uniquely optimal among all shapes
Generalizes to spheres in higher dimensions
Connected to eigenvalue problems and heat diffusion
The **Sobolev inequality** $\|f\|_{L^{n/(n-1)}} \le C_n \|\nabla f\|_{L^1}$ is a functional-analytic reformulation via the co-area formula, connecting geometry to PDE theory
prerequisites: Geometry (area, perimeter, curves in the plane)
Calculus of variations (extremal problems, Lagrange multipliers)

crossReferences.description: The area formula $A = \pi r^2$ and circumference $C = 2\pi r$ used to define Circle and verify the optimal isoperimetric ratio $1/(4\pi)$ are formalized in the Area of a Circle entry.
The isoperimetric equality $C^2 = 4\pi A$ proved in the Circumference from Area entry is the equality case of this theorem restricted to circles.
Pick's theorem relates area to lattice points for polygons. Both results connect perimeter/boundary information to enclosed area, though in different settings (continuous vs discrete).
The IBP formula for Fourier coefficients (ĉₙ(f') = in·ĉₙ(f)) is a key analytical ingredient in Hurwitz's Fourier-analytic proof of the isoperimetric inequality.
The Wirtinger inequality and Fourier framework entry provides the other key ingredient for the Fourier-analytic proof.
Fourier series provide the analytical machinery for Hurwitz's proof: the curve is decomposed into Fourier modes, and the isoperimetric deficit is expressed as a sum of squared coefficients.
The product-sum corollary of AM-GM (ab ≤ ((a+b)/2)²) proves the isoperimetric inequality for rectangles; the full theorem generalizes this to arbitrary curves.

The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is used in the parametric proof of the isoperimetric theorem: for a curve $(x(t), y(t))$ with period $T$, the area $A = \frac{1}{2}|\oint (x\,dy - y\,dx)|$ is bounded by applying Cauchy-Schwarz to the Fourier coefficients, yielding $4\pi A \leq L^2$. The Wirtinger inequality (a consequence of Cauchy-Schwarz for Fourier series) is the key analytical step

Green's theorem converts the isoperimetric problem from a double integral (area) to a line integral: $A = \frac{1}{2}\oint_C (x\,dy - y\,dx)$. This representation is essential for all analytic proofs of the isoperimetric inequality, as it expresses area purely in terms of the boundary curve — the same boundary whose length $L$ appears in the inequality $4\pi A \leq L^2$

Both are fundamental results about convex bodies: the isoperimetric theorem characterizes the optimal shape (circle/sphere), while Brouwer's fixed point theorem guarantees fixed points for continuous maps on convex sets. Both use compactness arguments — the isoperimetric theorem via the direct method of calculus of variations, Brouwer via algebraic topology

sections.title: Simple Closed Curves and Circle Definitions
sections.summary: Defines `SimpleClosedCurve` (perimeter $L > 0$, area $A \ge 0$) and `Circle` (radius $r > 0$) with derived `perimeter = 2\pi r$, `area = \pi r^2$, and coercion `Circle.toCurve`. Proves positivity of circle's perimeter and area.

sections.title: Isoperimetric Ratio
sections.summary: Defines the dimensionless ratio $\rho = A/L^2$ and the optimal value $1/(4\pi)$. Proves `circle_achieves_optimal_ratio`: every circle attains the theoretical maximum via algebraic computation (`field_simp` + `ring`).
sections.mathContext: Defines the dimensionless ratio $\rho = A/L^2$ and the optimal value $1/(4\pi)$. Proves `circle_achieves_optimal_ratio`: every circle attains the theoretical maximum via algebraic computation (`field_simp` + `ring`).

sections.title: Main Theorem: The Isoperimetric Inequality
sections.summary: Axiomatizes $4\pi A \le L^2$ for all simple closed curves. Derives the ratio form $A/L^2 \le 1/(4\pi)$ as a corollary. Documents why the proof is beyond current Mathlib (requires symmetrization, Fourier analysis, or Brunn-Minkowski).
sections.mathContext: Axiomatizes $4\pi A \le L^2$ for all simple closed curves. Derives the ratio form $A/L^2 \le 1/(4\pi)$ as a corollary.

sections.title: Equality Characterization
sections.summary: Defines `IsOptimal` ($4\pi A = L^2$) and proves circles satisfy it. Axiomatizes the converse: optimality implies circularity. This **rigidity** result is the key qualitative insight.
sections.mathContext: Defines `IsOptimal` ($4\$\pi$ A = L^2$) and proves circles satisfy it. Axiomatizes the converse: optimality implies circularity. This **rigidity** result is the key qualitative insight.

sections.title: Examples: Square vs Circle
sections.summary: Defines `Square` and `EquilateralTriangle`, computes their isoperimetric ratios ($1/16$ and $1/(12\sqrt{3})$ respectively), and proves both are strictly suboptimal compared to circles.
sections.mathContext: Formal definition: Defines `Square` and `EquilateralTriangle`, computes their isoperimetric ratios ($1/16$ and $1/(12\sqrt{3})$ respectively), and proves both are strictly suboptimal compared to circles.

sections.title: Higher-Dimensional Generalizations
sections.summary: States the 3D isoperimetric inequality $36\pi V^2 \le S^3$ (sphere is optimal) and the general $n$-dimensional form involving $\omega_n$, the volume of the unit $n$-ball.
sections.mathContext: States the 3D isoperimetric inequality $36\$\pi$ V^2 \le S^3$ (sphere is optimal) and the general $n$-dimensional form involving $\omega_n$, the volume of the unit $n$-ball.

sections.title: Applications and Connections
sections.summary: Discusses applications in physics (soap bubbles), biology (cell shapes), engineering (optimal tanks), and connections to Sobolev inequalities, concentration of measure, geometric measure theory, and optimal transport.
sections.mathContext: Discusses applications in physics (soap bubbles), biology (cell shapes), engineering (optimal tanks), and connections to Sobolev inequalities, concentration of measure, geometric measure theory, and optimal transport.

conclusion.summary: The isoperimetric theorem is a fundamental optimization result showing the circle's unique role in geometry. It has inspired vast generalizations in geometric measure theory and differential geometry.
conclusion.implications: Applications range from physics (soap bubbles, crystal growth) to engineering (optimal design) to biology (cell shapes). The theorem generalizes to Riemannian manifolds and metric spaces.
